title: Visible haematuria with clot retention
scenario: A 64-year-old heavy smoker presents with visible haematuria and inability to void. He is taking an antiplatelet agent after coronary stenting. He is uncomfortable, with a palpable bladder. No trauma is reported.
tasks: State the immediate priorities and how you would relieve clot retention safely.
List the key history, examination findings, and initial investigations.
Construct the differential diagnosis and explain why urothelial malignancy and renal malignancy require evaluation.
Explain how you would coordinate antiplatelet decisions with cardiology rather than stopping treatment reflexively.
discussion_points: Assess haemodynamic stability, blood loss, pain, urine output, and renal function.
Urgent urological assessment; large-bore three-way catheter and irrigation may be needed when appropriate and safe, with escalation if drainage fails.
Visible haematuria warrants evaluation of both lower and upper urinary tracts; antiplatelet therapy does not remove the need to investigate the cause.
Recent coronary stenting makes interruption of antiplatelet therapy a high-risk multidisciplinary decision.

title: Antenatal hydronephrosis in a newborn boy
scenario: A male neonate is noted to have bilateral hydroureteronephrosis on antenatal and postnatal ultrasound. The bladder appears thick-walled and the urinary stream is poor.
tasks: Give the most important diagnosis and two alternatives.
Describe immediate assessment of renal function, urine output, infection, and bladder drainage.
Explain the role of ultrasound and voiding cystourethrography in the work-up.
Outline the principles of definitive management and long-term renal follow-up.
discussion_points: Posterior urethral valves are a key diagnosis in a boy with bilateral upper-tract dilatation and bladder outlet features.
Stabilize the infant and involve pediatric urology early; assess renal function and urinary infection.
Imaging choice and timing should follow specialist assessment and local pediatric pathways.
Long-term follow-up is important because renal and bladder dysfunction may persist after valve ablation.
